c.tagline: Ancient crossroads city rebuilding beneath the Hindu Kush.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are not used; agree the fare with the driver before departure.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be slow or inconsistent outside central districts; foreign visitors typically also contact their embassy, employer's security office, or hotel for assistance.

avoid.reason: Foreign governments advise against all travel to Kabul; in particular avoid crowds, government and military sites, places of worship at prayer times, and frequently targeted areas such as the Dasht-e-Barchi district.

Risk of attacks, arbitrary detention and kidnapping exists citywide, and Taliban-imposed rules severely restrict women's dress, movement and activities — any visit requires professional security arrangements.

hood_desc: Kabul's diplomatic quarter of walled compounds, embassies and NGO guesthouses; the most orderly and heavily secured area, favored by diplomats, aid workers and business travelers.

The commercial heart of the city, packed with shops, restaurants and the carpet-and-curio stalls of Chicken Street; convenient and lively, suited to travelers who want to be near markets and eateries.
A northwestern residential belt rising toward the hilltop InterContinental hotel, offering panoramic views and a quieter mix of guesthouses; suited to those wanting calm with easy access downtown.
A low-key residential district of apartment blocks and NGO compounds west of the center; suited to longer-stay aid workers and business visitors wanting an understated base.
University district near Kabul University and the National Museum, with bookshops and student cafes; suited to travelers interested in academic and cultural sites.
lodging: Darya Village Hotel and Business Park

water.note: Groundwater is heavily contaminated; only drink bottled water and avoid tap water even for brushing teeth.

sys.n: Milli Bus (state-run Kabul city bus network)

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; there is no card or app-based payment system. Shared taxis and minibuses charge a fixed per-seat cash fare set by route.
transit.hours: Buses and shared taxis generally run roughly 6am-8pm; there is little to no public transport after dark, so travelers typically rely on hired cars or hotel-arranged drivers at night.
transit.note: Kabul has no metro, tram or rail transit; the state Milli Bus network and privately run shared taxis/minibuses cover the city, but most foreign visitors use hired cars with drivers rather than public transit.

airport.name: Hamid Karzai International Airport (KBL)
airport.drive: 20-30 min from downtown, longer at security checkpoints

tip.r: Not traditionally expected at local eateries; rounding up taxi fares or a small tip for hotel staff, guides and drivers is appreciated but not obligatory.

food.name: Kabuli Pulao
food.desc: Afghanistan's national dish: long-grain rice steamed over lamb and crowned with caramelised carrot slivers, raisins and slivered almonds.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing name for traditional pulao and charcoal kebabs.

places.name: Hakeem Restaurant
places.note: Famous for qabuli palau and pacha soup; a highway institution.

places.name: Bukhara Restaurant
places.note: Calmer upscale room; a sit-down version of the classic rice plate.

food.name: Mantu
food.desc: Thin-skinned steamed dumplings of minced beef and onion, dressed with garlicky yoghurt, split-pea and tomato sauce and dried mint.

places.name: Ziyafat Restaurant
places.note: Mantu with tomato and chickpea sauce is one of its star plates.

places.name: Bukhara Restaurant
places.note: Neat, well-run dining room popular for dumplings and rice.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Homestyle mantu alongside the kebab grill.

food.name: Ashak
food.desc: Kabul's leek dumplings: pasta parcels stuffed with chopped gandana greens under yoghurt, meat sauce and a heavy dust of dried mint.

places.name: Ziyafat Restaurant
places.note: Serves the vegetarian ashak version as a signature.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Reliable traditional kitchen doing both ashak and mantu.

places.name: Bukhara Restaurant
places.note: Good for a slower meal with the full dumpling range.

food.name: Bolani
food.desc: Thin pan-fried flatbread folded around potato, leek or pumpkin and cut into wedges, eaten with mint yoghurt; Kabul's great street snack.

places.name: Mandawi Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Griddles turning out potato and leek bolani through the day.

places.name: Chicken Street snack stalls
places.note: Easy walk-up bolani and tea near the main shopping strip.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down bolani if you would rather not eat on the street.

food.name: Afghan Kebab
food.desc: Skewers of lamb, minced chapli patties or karayi cooked over charcoal and served on naan with raw onion, dried mint and lemon.

places.name: Ziyafat Restaurant
places.note: Kebabs are the headline order; polished service at local prices.

places.name: Hakeem Restaurant
places.note: Kebabs and soup served to travellers around the clock.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Charcoal grill running all evening; high turnover of fresh meat.

food.name: Firni
food.desc: Chilled milk pudding thickened with rice flour, scented with cardamom and rosewater and scattered with pistachio; the standard Kabul dessert.

places.name: Bukhara Restaurant
places.note: Full dessert list; firni served properly cold in shallow dishes.

places.name: Mandawi Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Trays of firni and jelabi sold by weight from the sweet sellers.

places.name: Ziyafat Restaurant
places.note: Rounds off the kebab and dumpling meal with milk puddings.

food.name: Green Tea (Chai Sabz)
food.desc: Cardamom-scented green tea poured endlessly from a pot with sugared almonds alongside; alcohol is banned nationwide, so tea is the social drink.

places.name: Chai khanas of Mandawi
places.note: Traditional teahouses where the pot arrives before you order food.

places.name: Bilal Restaurant
places.note: Green tea comes with every meal, refilled without asking.

places.name: Bukhara Restaurant
places.note: Quiet room for a long tea session; strictly no alcohol.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink shaken with dried mint and sometimes cucumber and served ice-cold; the standard non-alcoholic partner to rich kebab.

places.name: Ziyafat Restaurant
places.note: Jugs of doogh brought out with the kebab platters.

places.name: Hakeem Restaurant
places.note: Cold doogh is the drink of choice with the pulao here.

places.name: Mandawi Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Street sellers pour it by the glass from chilled churns.

landmarks: Darul Aman Palace
A grand neoclassical palace on Kabul's outskirts, scarred by decades of war and recently restored, symbolizing Afghanistan's turbulent modern history.
Bagh-e Babur (Babur's Gardens)
A serene terraced garden built for Mughal emperor Babur, offering shady walkways, fountains, and his own tomb amid Kabul's dusty cityscape.
Bala Hissar
An ancient hilltop fortress overlooking Kabul, with walls dating back over a thousand years, witness to countless sieges and empires.
Pul-e Khishti Mosque
Kabul's largest and oldest mosque, its blue-tiled dome and minarets forming a striking centerpiece along the Kabul River in the old city.
Id Gah Mosque
A historic mosque with elegant white arches and columns, traditionally hosting Kabul's largest Eid prayer gatherings for over a century.
National Museum of Afghanistan
Home to thousands of rare Bactrian, Gandharan, and Islamic artifacts that survived war and looting, chronicling Afghanistan's rich crossroads history.
Kart-e Sakhi Shrine
A revered Shia shrine with a gleaming blue-and-gold dome nestled below Kabul's hills, drawing pilgrims especially during Nowruz celebrations.
Shah-Do Shamshira Mosque
Nicknamed the 'Mosque of the King of Two Swords,' this ornate riverside mosque with twin minarets is one of Kabul's most photographed buildings.
TV Hill (Kabul)
A hillside viewpoint crowned with a television tower, offering sweeping panoramic vistas across Kabul's sprawling, mountain-ringed valley.
Kabul Zoo
One of the region's oldest zoos and a resilient survivor of decades of conflict, remaining a beloved family destination in the capital.

train.note: Afghanistan has no passenger railway reaching Kabul. The country's only rail lines are short freight links at the borders - Hairatan in the north and the Khaf-Herat line to Iran in the west (with a new Herat-Mashhad passenger service) - none of which serve the capital. From Kabul you travel by road or air.

bus.note: There are no scheduled international coach lines with online booking. Overland travellers use shared buses and taxis from Kabul toward the Pakistan border at Torkham (for Peshawar) and, via Kandahar, to Spin Boldak (for Quetta), or westward through Herat to the Iranian border at Islam Qala (for Mashhad). Long-distance domestic buses leave from terminals such as Sarai Shomali. Check current security and visa rules carefully before travelling.

ferry.note: Afghanistan is landlocked, so there are no ferries.
